newsitem.title: DEMOCRATIC REPUBLIC OF CONGO: Kinshasa protests flare after Kabila detains rival.
newsitem.headline: Kinshasa protests flare after Kabila detains rival.

text.p: Laurent Kabila's soldiers fired into the air on Friday to disperse crowds protesting in the capital Kinshasa at the overnight detention of veteran opposition leader Etienne Tshisekedi, witnesses said.
Dozens of rioters threw stones, set vehicles alight and chanted anti-Kabila slogans in parts of Kinshasa, capital of the Democratic Republic of the Congo, the former Zaire.
Soldiers took away Tshisekedi, a thorn in the side first of ousted dictator Mobutu Sese Seko and now of Kabila, after he defied a ban to address a political gathering on Thursday.
He was released after questioning on Friday along with members of his family and associates who had also been held.
An angry mob of around 100 people marched in the city centre. Some threw stones at bystanders who refused to join in.
In the Limete suburb where Tshisekedi lives, his supporters torched vehicles, vandalised a petrol station, and burnt tyres on the main Boulevard Lumumba.
"The armed forces came -- they fired into the air to disperse the crowd," said one witness standing beside a smouldering vehicle.
Military patrols surveyed Limete through the morning.

Next-door neighbours said Tshisekedi and his wife had returned home in the early morning, but soldiers were still stationed outside their front gate and took away foreign television journalists who tried to film the scene.
The veteran opposition leader and one-time Zairean premier was taken from his home hours after addressing thousands of students in defiance of a government ban on political activity.
"He was questioned for a long time. We are disappointed. They want to light the fire," said Adrien Phongo, secretary general of Tshisekedi's Union for Democracy and Social Progress (UDPS) party.
Tshisekedi was the main domestic opponent to Mobutu, whom Kabila and his Alliance of Democratic Forces for the Liberation of Congo toppled in May after a seven-month civil war.
Named premier by a national democracy conference but sacked by Mobutu, he never accepted his dismissal and his supporters still refer to him as the prime minister.
Kabila has banned political parties, marches and gatherings and has alienated opposition followers by excluding Tshisekedi from his new government.

The ban has undermined support for Kabila, who was seen as a hero for ending Mobutu's 32-year corrupt rule. Troops broke up earlier marches by Tshisekedi loyalists with teargas or by firing in the air.
Ironically, Tshisekedi's address at Kinshasa university had been full of conciliatory messages.
He announced that he had held talks with Kabila's Alliance to "harmonize conflicting views" on the institutions of the renamed Democratic Republic of the Congo.

Tshisekedi said his new contacts with the Alliance could lead to a new transitional government to prepare for elections promised for 1999, and that he could soon meet Kabila for the first time since he declared himself president.
"We gave a message of appeasement and they have answered that with force," an adviser said after the arrest.
Government spokesmen were unavailable for comment.
